deep.reconstruction:
This page contains no mathematics. It continues the previous page's narrative notes, in German, on the wars of Alexander's successors (the Diadochi), probably lecture or reading notes on ancient history. Content, in order:

1. Antigonus recalls his son Demetrius from Athens (spring 307 BC) to begin a formal war against Ptolemaeus, who had recently subdued Cyprus.
2. Ptolemaeus has 60 ships at Cyprus (at Salamis, under his brother Menelaus) and comes himself with 140 more. Demetrius comes with 160 ships.
3. A great naval battle lasts almost the whole day. This is the battle of Salamis in Cyprus, 306 BC. Demetrius wins. Almost the whole Egyptian fleet is destroyed or captured, and Ptolemaeus barely escapes to Egypt with the 8 ships he has left.
4. Antigonus now takes the royal title. The sentence continues onto the next page: in Syria at Antigonia; Ptolemaeus also takes the title.

The only numbers are fleet sizes (60, 140, 160, 8), with no computation beyond the implied total of 60 + 140 = 200 ships for Ptolemaeus. The hand and content suggest school or student history notes bound into the bundle, not Gauss's mathematical work. Authorship is unsure.
errors: No mathematical errors, since there is no mathematics. Historically, Diodorus (XX.47-52) gives Demetrius a somewhat larger fleet than 160 (figures around 180 warships are usually cited). The details of Ptolemy's 140 ships plus Menelaus' 60, and Ptolemy's escape with 8 ships, match the standard account.

results.what: Narrative account of the naval battle of Salamis in Cyprus (306 BC) and the Diadochi assuming royal titles
results.usually_credited_to: Diodorus Siculus XX.47-53; Plutarch, Life of Demetrius

deep.surprise_reason: The page is purely historical narrative copied or noted from standard sources on the Diadochi. It has no mathematical content, and the handwriting may not even be Gauss's.

checkable.asserts: Ptolemy's total fleet (60 at Cyprus plus 140 he brought) was 200 ships.
Number of Ptolemaic ships lost or captured if only 8 escaped (implied, not stated on the page).

transcription_corrections: Line 2-3: 'der früher[?] aber[?] Cypros unterworfen hatte' more likely reads 'der sich eben Cypros unterworfen hatte'.
'Königlichen Titel' appears written as 'Königlichen'. The line ends 'in Syrien zu Antigo-', continuing as 'nia' on the next page.
Underlined proper names (Ptolemaeus, Cypros, Demetrius, Antigonus, Syrien) are emphasized in the original; 'Ptolemaeus' is spelled variously (Ptolämaeus/Ptolemaeus).
